Tentmaker
TENT-may-ker
noun
From tent (Old French tente, from Latin tendere, “to stretch”) and maker; rendering the Greek skēnopoios, a worker in the coarse goats’-hair cloth and leather of which travellers’ tents were made.

Biblical Definition

A tentmaker cuts and stitches the heavy goats’-hair cloth called cilicium — the very fabric of Paul’s native Cilicia — into tents, awnings, and coverings. It is hard on the hands and it smells; and it is the trade the LORD gave the greatest missionary in the history of the church. Coming to Corinth, Paul found Aquila and Priscilla, “and because he was of the same craft, he abode with them, and wrought: for by their occupation they were tentmakers” (Act 18:3). He preached in the synagogue every sabbath and worked at the bench through the week. He was not ashamed to say so, holding up his hands before the Ephesian elders: “ye yourselves know, that these hands have ministered unto my necessities, and to them that were with me” (Act 20:34). This was no denial of the minister’s right to support — Paul argues that right at length elsewhere — but a voluntary waiving of it, that no man might say he preached for hire. From the same conviction he laid down the rule for every congregation: “if any would not work, neither should he eat” (2Th 3:10), and pressed the quiet, unspectacular ideal: “that ye study to be quiet, and to do your own business, and to work with your own hands” (1Th 4:11). The apostle to the Gentiles kept a needle and an awl, and the church has never been allowed to forget it.

Webster 1828 Definition

One who makes tents; the trade of Paul, Aquila, and Priscilla at Corinth.

expand to see more

TENTMAKER, one whose occupation is the making of tents from cloth or skins.

Rendering the Greek skēnopoios, a worker in goats’-hair cloth and leather.

The coarse cloth called cilicium took its name from Paul’s own province of Cilicia.

Paul, Aquila, and Priscilla shared the craft at Corinth (Act 18:3).

By it Paul supported himself and his company rather than burden the churches (Act 20:34).

Key Scripture

Act 18:3 — "And because he was of the same craft, he abode with them, and wrought: for by their occupation they were tentmakers."

Act 20:34 — "Yea, ye yourselves know, that these hands have ministered unto my necessities, and to them that were with me."

2Th 3:10 — "For even when we were with you, this we commanded you, that if any would not work, neither should he eat."

1Th 4:11 — "And that ye study to be quiet, and to do your own business, and to work with your own hands, as we commanded you;"

Modern Corruption

Paul's awl rebukes two opposite errors: the hireling who preaches for gain, and the idler who will not work at all.

expand to see more

The first live corruption is the professionalised religion Paul deliberately refused to look like. There were teachers at Corinth and Crete alike who trafficked in doctrine “for filthy lucre’s sake” (Tit 1:11), and the modern platform has multiplied them: the conference circuit, the donation appeal timed to the emotional crescendo, the ministry whose books are its real business. The tentmaker is the standing answer. A man who can feed himself by his hands has removed the strongest temptation to trim his preaching, and the congregation that watches him stitch through the week knows exactly what his sermon is not for sale. Note carefully that Paul never denied the labourer his hire; he waived a right he had, which is a different and higher thing than pretending the right does not exist.

The opposite corruption is the idleness Paul had to rebuke in the same letter that gave us the rule. Some at Thessalonica were “working not at all, but are busybodies” (2Th 3:11), spiritualising their laziness with talk of the Lord’s return. The apostolic command is blunt and unfashionable: if a man will not work, let him not eat. This is not a denial of mercy to the widow, the orphan, the sick, or the man who cannot find work — Scripture is loud in their defence — but it is a refusal to subsidise the able-bodied unwilling. Between the hireling and the idler stands the tentmaker: a man who preaches for nothing and eats what his own hands have earned.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

A maker of goats'-hair tents; Paul's trade and the model of self-supporting ministry.

expand to see more

Tentmaker — Greek skēnopoios, a worker in tent-cloth and leather.

Tent traces to Latin tendere, to stretch.

Cilician goats’-hair cloth was the standard material — Paul’s home industry.

At Corinth the craft joined Paul to Aquila and Priscilla (Act 18:3).

The bench funded the mission: these hands have ministered unto my necessities (Act 20:34).

Usage

"A tentmaking ministry is not a lesser ministry; it was the apostle’s own."

"If any would not work, neither should he eat — apostolic, not merely proverbial."

"Paul waived his right to support; he never denied that the right existed."
